proposed_edges.relationship: The global held to be a human-centred frame, “insufficient (but not unnecessary)” once human history meets geological time, and Big History’s hope that large-scale history yields “global citizenship” questioned (2015–22)
proposed_edges.map_label: Globe and planet: amending world and Big History, 2015–22
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words. Tanner Lectures (Yale, 18–19 February 2015; official text read in part, unpaginated), lecture II: "this assumption that thinking on large scales leads to a sense of human solidarity or 'global citizenship' has found a resurgent expression in a branch of historical scholarship that calls itself Big (or sometime Deep) History"; in David Christian's hands "the history of the human species merges seamlessly with the history of 'humanity'"; Christian "directly cites the world-history pioneer William McNeill's 1986 presidential address" (McNeill's words are given only as Christian quotes them). A note on Smail ("I agree, and I do not") announces "Some Friendly Amendments": an amendment, not a rejection. The Review of Politics (2022), his introduction, read in full: the convergence of human and natural histories "has rendered insufficient (but not unnecessary)" the framework of empire, race and global capitalism; labels "such as 'modern' or 'global' now have to be thought together with the much larger-scale units of geological time"; "The global is anthropocentric while the planet de-centers and provincializes the human" (p. 593); his response calls capital and empire "a necessary but insufficient framework" (p. 610). Context: the 2014 Toynbee Prize "for his contributions to global history" (university biography), presented with his lecture "From Globalization to Global Warming" on 3 January 2015 (lecture unread). Reception: Getachew (2022, p. 601) calls the planetary turn "a significant departure from and challenge to" his own anticolonial and postcolonial traditions. edge_124 (post → global, critique) records the group's 2000 critique of Eurocentric global narratives; this is a different, later claim about scale.

proposed_edges.relationship: The distinction between human and natural history, defended “from Hegel and Marx to Croce and Collingwood”, held to collapse under anthropogenic climate change: the starting point of his climate work (2009–22)
proposed_edges.map_label: Against the human/natural divide of Croce and Collingwood, 2009–22
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words. The Review of Politics (2022), introduction, read in full: "This collapse of the distinction, defended over the last two centuries by philosophers ranging from Hegel and Marx to Croce and Collingwood, between humanist histories of humans and their natural histories provides the starting point for my book" (p. 593). The 2009 essay's first thesis (existing reading, p. 201): anthropogenic climate change spells "the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History"; the essay was read in full in an earlier pass (2026-10-14; see its source note), but the passages then recorded (pp. 199, 201, 205–208, 212, 219–222) do not include its discussion of Croce and Collingwood, which was not rechecked in this wave and is not quoted. The edge rests on the 2022 paragraph. Richard Staley (2024, read) summarises the later book's view that postcolonial scholars "inherited a strong human/non-human nature distinction from philosophers of history who argued that history is limited to human affairs" (p. 658), while calling the first thesis "one of the most problematic arguments" of the 2009 essay (see the science critique). This concerns only the human/natural distinction of idealist philosophy of history; it is not the developmental "historicism" ("first in Europe, then elsewhere") that Provincializing Europe criticised (edge_914), a different sense of the word.

proposed_edges.relationship: Critics of the four theses question the “species” category, holding inequalities within humanity integral to the ecological crisis (Malm and Hornborg, 2014; abstract only; that they address him is his report), and whether a divide between human and natural history ever existed (the environmental historian LeCain, 2016); Chakrabarty answers that capital is “a necessary but insufficient framework” (2015–22)
proposed_edges.map_label: Species or capital? Critics of the four theses, 2014–16 (Malm and Hornborg abstract only)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Named critics drawn from environmental history, where the 2009 essay was taken up (edge_918). Andreas Malm and Alf Hornborg, "The Geology of Mankind?" (Anthropocene Review, 2014): abstract only; it "questions the use of the species category in the Anthropocene narrative and argues that it is analytically flawed, as well as inimical to action", and holds that "Intra-species inequalities are part and parcel of the current ecological crisis". The abstract does not name Chakrabarty; that they "took me to task" is his own report (2016 response, p. 108, existing reading; Tanner lecture I, read, whose note cites them for the "capitalocene" objection). They write as human ecologists, not environmental historians. Timothy LeCain, an environmental historian (Whose Anthropocene?, 2016, existing reading): "it becomes reasonable to ask whether there was ever a divide in the first place" (p. 17). His answers: geological names do not "assign moral responsibility" (Tanner lecture I); "My book does not deny the role of capitalism", capital being "a necessary but insufficient framework" (Review of Politics, 2022, p. 610). Pitts (2022, read) finds his reasons for holding the Capitalocene "at arm's length" in "fascinating and productive" tension (p. 607). Balance from the field: Atte Arffman, reviewing the 2021 book in Environment and History (2022, read), writes that "not many have delved as deep as Chakrabarty does". The endpoint locates named interventions; it does not make them environmental history's verdict.

proposed_edges.relationship: A historian of science finds the 2009 thesis of a collapsing human/nature divide “one of the most problematic arguments”, since histories of climate such as Golinski’s had stressed the link between human and nature, and the later politics too abstract (Staley, 2024)
proposed_edges.map_label: Staley on the novelty of the divide, 2024
proposed_edges.evidence_note: One named reader, read in full: Richard Staley, review of One Planet, Many Worlds (British Journal for the History of Science 57:4, 2024): "One of the most problematic arguments of The Climate of History was its assertion that 'Anthropogenic Explanations of Climate Change Spell the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History'. This impression of the novelty of the Anthropocene might have been dispelled by attention to the considerable work stressing the common link between human and nature in concepts of climate, such as Jan Golinski's British Weather and the Climate of Enlightenment (2007)" (p. 658); "without engaging in significant emerging literatures on the history and politics of climate science and governance policies, we are left with the somewhat abstract entreaty" (p. 659). Kept in his appraisal: Chakrabarty "has responded to critics and sharpened his account" (p. 657), and the 2023 book is "more appropriately concerned with the recent origins of a separation between humans and nature" (p. 658). Golinski is named only by Staley. The 2023 book is unread. One reviewer, not the field's verdict.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Calling of History (2015) reads Jadunath Sarkar’s “imperial liberalism” and his public quarrels with nationalist historians over objectivity and sources, asking when a society values the “cloistered life” of history, as Joshi and the publisher report
proposed_edges.map_label: Jadunath Sarkar and the public life of history, 2015 (as reviewed)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The book is unread; its argument is given as its readers state it. Publisher's description: through "more than twelve hundred letters", historians in colonial India "formulated the basic concepts and practices of the field via vigorous—and at times bitter and hurtful—debates in the public sphere". Girija Joshi's review (Práticas da História 3, 2016, read in full): Sarkar appeared "to be a spokesperson for what Chakrabarty calls 'imperial liberalism' (p. 49)", while his rivals of the Bharat Itihas Samshodhak Mandal valued "an ability to understand 'the spirit' of the source" (p. 152); the book asks under what circumstances "a society values the 'objectivity' ... of historical research", and when the public life of history defers to its "cloistered life" (book p. 6; review p. 153). Suman Seth (History and Theory, 2017; abstract only) reads it as "a defense of rationalist history in the face of contemporary threats posed by the rise of a politics of identity in India". A contribution to the history of colonial and national historiography in India; no strand is assigned.

verification.note: Read in full. Held in Lisbon, January 2020. His Marxist teachers were uneasy at his evidence of conflict between Hindu and Muslim workers, "For, as readers of E. P. Thompson, they assumed that there was a story waiting to be written about 'the making of the Indian working class'"; the paper appeared in Past and Present (pp. 26–27; n. 1, Past & Present 91, 1981).
